title: Not yet
hookLine: rushing forgiveness can hurt; healing keeps its own time

lines: A CAST ON A BROKEN WRIST.
cards: A broken wrist goes into a cast, and nobody asks it to throw a ball the next morning. Everyone can see the plaster. Everyone understands the bone needs time, and that pushing it too soon can break it again.
Hurts of the heart don't come with a cast.

Nobody can see them, so forgiveness sometimes gets asked for on a schedule: at the funeral, across the holiday table, the day after the apology, by someone who means well and wants things smooth again.

teach.b: Ecclesiastes, the Bible's book of seasons, opens its list of times this way: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven."
And on that list, among planting and building and dancing, is this: "a time to heal." Not a moment. A time.
Healing gets its own season, and the list doesn't say how long a season is.

Robert Enright, whose list came yesterday, describes forgiveness as a process with phases, and his first phase is uncovering: looking honestly at the hurt and the anger before trying to do anything with them.

teach.h: A LID IS NOT A RELEASE.
teach.b: It's hard to release something you haven't looked at yet. A forgiveness pushed out too early, to keep the peace or please someone else, can turn into a lid on the hurt rather than a release of it.

The words get said; the wound underneath can stay open. That's why, in Enright's order, the looking comes first. Then a line from the Psalms: "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds."
Healing comes with binding up: the wound is wrapped and given time. A bandage isn't a refusal to get better; it's part of how getting better happens. So not yet isn't the opposite of forgiveness.
It can be the first part of it.
It's a cast on the wrist while the bone does its slow, invisible work.

how: Forgiveness counselors who follow Robert Enright's process model begin by helping people uncover the hurt and anger, and let the decision to forgive come later, in its own time.

o: refusing to forgive at all, no matter what happens
putting off an apology you know you owe someone
not ready to forgive yet, which isn't the same as never

games.q: the order of healing — tap the pairs.

s: Ecclesiastes says how long the time to heal should take
it says there is "a time to heal" and never says how long a season is.
Enright's process begins by looking at the hurt and anger
his first phase is uncovering, before any decision to forgive.
not yet can be the first part of forgiveness, like a cast while the bone heals.

games.q: a friend was badly hurt just weeks ago. at a family gathering, a relative tells her to forgive and move on, right now. what fits today's teaching?
o: forgive on the spot to keep the peace.
not yet is allowed; healing keeps its own time.
games.why: Ecclesiastes gives "a time to heal," and Enright starts with uncovering the hurt. a forgiveness pushed out too early can be a lid, not a release. not yet is not never.

practice: Choose one hurt that's still fresh, one you're not ready to forgive, and instead of forgiving it, sit beside it the way you'd sit beside a friend in a cast: not fixing, not pushing, just keeping it company, with a hand on your chest or lap if that helps.
In your head, say two words to it, not yet, and let that be enough for the whole sit.

wordCard.voice: Not yet. A time to heal comes before a time to let go; not yet can be the first part of forgiveness, not its opposite. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a time, a season. the word repeated through the list in Ecclesiastes 3.

carryVoice: Your line: not yet is allowed. Healing keeps its own season, however long that is. See you tomorrow.
